captions: A promise before we start.

Every idea here, I'll explain with something you
already
know.
We'll use a method called ADEPT — analogy, diagram,
example, plain words, then the technical term.

Today's topic: daily trading algorithms. How
machines actually trade,
and the India reality.
None of this is investment advice. It's a way
of thinking.
Here's a puzzle.
An order hits the exchange in the blink of
an eye.
Nobody clicked a button. A rule did — a
computer following instructions, with no emotion.

By financial year twenty twenty-four, twelve point
eight percent
of N S E cash-market turnover was classified as
algo.
That's one scoped number, not a claim about all
trading.
So what is that rule really doing? Let's build
it up, from the very beginning.
Part one.
What a trading rule actually does — the simple
loop hiding inside every bot.
Think of a vending machine.
You meet its one condition — insert the coin
— and it acts, the same way every single
time, with no mood and no hesitation.
A trading algorithm has a loop just like that:
it takes in data, forms a signal, checks risk,
sends an order, and receives a fill.
Here's a real case. Suppose I decide: if the
price crosses a line I chose, buy exactly one

lot. The computer watches every tick, and the
instant
that line is crossed, the order goes — just
one, exactly as written.

In plain words, an algorithm turns incoming data
into
controlled orders, and then keeps watching itself.
The technical name for all of this is algorithmic

trading, and the authenticated pipe it sends orders
through
is called direct market access, or D M A.
Now, not everything fast is an algo.

Picture a highway: some cars drive themselves, some
sit
in a fast lane near the toll, and some
rented the on-ramp.
Those are three different things. On N S E

cash market in financial year twenty twenty-four,
algo was

twelve point eight percent of turnover, while
co-location was

thirty-four point three percent — and co-location is
not
an algo share.
In the United States, the I M F put
algo near seventy percent of equity trading — a
U S figure, not India.

Here's the example that matters: a co-located order
can
still be placed by a human.

Plainly: automation, speed, and access are three
separate choices.

The technical point — high-frequency trading is just
a
fast subset; the India-wide share stays unverified.
Part two.
The strategies.

These charts use illustrative, synthetic data —
never a
backtest, never a promise.
Our first strategy is momentum.
Think of pushing a child on a swing —
you don't fight it, you push while it's already
moving your way.
To see the trend, we draw two moving averages
on the price: a fast one that reacts quickly,
and a slow one that reacts gently.
Here's the rule in action. When the fast line
crosses above the slow line, the recent trend has
turned up, so the algorithm can go long; when
the fast line crosses back below, the trend has
faded, and it exits. Notice it never tries to
catch the exact bottom — it waits for the
turn to be confirmed.
In plain words, you're riding a move that has
already begun, and letting it carry you.
The technical name is trend, or momentum, trading —
and its failure mode is chop: a flat, sideways
market that fakes you long and short, again and
again, paying costs each time.
The next strategy believes the opposite of momentum.
Think of a rubber band — stretch it too
far, and it wants to snap back.

To measure the stretch, we draw volatility bands
around
a moving average: an upper band and a lower
band that widen when the market gets wild.
For example, when price pokes below the lower band,
and a momentum gauge like R S I looks
washed out, the rule may bet on a bounce
back toward the middle.

In plain words, you're betting that an unusually
large
move returns toward its own average.
The technical name is mean reversion — and its
danger is the one thing it can't handle: a

genuine trend, where cheap simply keeps getting
cheaper, and
the band breaks instead of holding.
Our third strategy waits for a build-up.
Think of water behind a dam — pressure gathers
quietly, and then it escapes all at once.
On the chart, we take the first stretch of
the session and mark its highest high and lowest
low. That box is called the opening range.
Here's the example. If price pushes above the top
of the box, the rule buys the breakout, and
immediately places a stop just below — the exit
is decided before the entry.

In plain words, you're trading the exact moment
price
escapes a quiet range and starts to run.

The technical name is the opening-range breakout —
and

its classic failure is the false breakout, where
price
pokes out, sucks everyone in, and snaps right back,
often on a news gap.
This next one is different — it isn't about
what to buy, but how to buy it.
Imagine you have to buy a huge quantity. Slam
it in at once and you'll push the price

against yourself; instead you take small sips, so
you
don't spook the market.
On the chart, a V W A P line

traces the volume-weighted average price — a fair
benchmark
for the day — and your child orders try
to track it.
For example, one big parent order of a thousand

lots is chopped into twenty small slices, released
through
the day so each blends into normal volume.

In plain words, this is execution: quietly cutting
your
own footprint, not predicting direction at all.
The technical names are V W A P and
T W A P execution; the risks are market

impact and information leakage — letting others see
what
you're doing.
Here's a cleverer cousin of mean reversion.

Think of two dancers who almost always move
together;
you stop watching each one, and just watch the
gap between them.
On the chart, we track the spread between two
related stocks, and turn it into a z-score —
a number that says how unusual today's gap is.

For example, when that z-score stretches past two,
the
rule buys the cheap leg and shorts the expensive
leg, betting the gap closes.

In plain words, you're trading the relationship, not
the
market direction.

The technical name is statistical arbitrage, or
pairs trading
— and its real danger is a relationship that
simply breaks.
Now, who is on the other side of all
these trades?
Often a market maker — think of a shopkeeper
who'll always buy from you at one price and
sell at a slightly higher one.
The picture: the maker posts a bid and an
ask around fair value, on both sides at once.
For example, if both a buyer and a seller
trade with those quotes, the maker keeps the little
gap between them — the spread — while carefully
managing leftover inventory.
In plain words, they get paid to provide liquidity,
not to predict direction.

The technical risk is adverse selection — being
picked
off by someone who knows the price is about
to move.
The last strategy is the closest thing to a
free lunch — and it usually isn't.

Arbitrage is like buying mangoes cheaper in one
bazaar
to sell them dearer in another, at the same
moment.

The picture: compare two prices for the same
underlying
value — say a stock's cash price against its
futures price.
For example, buy the cheaper leg and sell the
dearer leg, and lock the gap — but only
if it beats funding, borrowing, taxes, and fees.
In plain words, these are tiny, locked gaps, chased
instantly by very fast competitors.

The technical name is cash-futures arbitrage, and
its risks
are basis, legging, and funding.
Part three.
The India reality.
A bot doesn't run in a vacuum — it
runs inside a broker and an exchange rulebook.
Think of a driving licence and a number plate
— for your bot.
The rulebook has dates, a speed cap, an identity,
and controls.
Here are the pieces. S E B I issued

the framework on the fourth of February twenty
twenty-five,
and it applies to all brokers from the first
of April twenty twenty-six.
The example threshold: at or below ten orders per
second, an A P I algo gets a generic
Algo I D; above it, the algo must be
registered. Access needs a static I P and two-factor
login.

Plainly, every bot must be identified, rate-limited,
and supervised
— the broker is the principal.

Technically, that's the S E B I retail-algo
framework,
with an exchange kill switch and a five-year audit
trail.
Now the part that decides everything: costs.
Every trade leaks a little, like a slightly leaky
bucket.
On the chart, gross returns fall into smaller net
returns as trading picks up.

For example: securities-transaction tax of zero
point zero five
percent on futures, zero point one five percent on
options, plus about twenty rupees a broker order and
eighteen percent G S T — that's a Zerodha
example, not every broker.

Plainly, automation is not an edge; costs decide
whether
high turnover can survive.
The sobering technical fact: a S E B I

study found ninety-three percent of over one crore
individual

futures-and-options traders lost money across
financial years twenty twenty-two
to twenty-four — losses above one point eight lakh
crore rupees. That's F and O traders, not algo
users.
Part four.
Building and running one.
The code is the easy part; the controls are
what make it a system.
So how do you actually build one?
Picture a factory line — with a foreman watching,
and a big red emergency stop within reach.
The line runs in order: market data comes in,
it's validated, a signal forms, risk checks it, an
order-and-risk system shapes it, the broker A P I
sends it, the exchange fills it, and monitoring plus
an end-of-day review close the loop.

For example, every hand-off should be observable —
at
any moment you can answer what data arrived, which
check approved it, and which order actually left. If
you can't answer that, you can't safely debug it.
In plain words, the strategy code is just one
part; the controls are what make it a real
system.
The technical pieces are the O M S and
R M S, reconciliation of intent against reality, and
a kill switch that is tested — not decorative.
Before you risk real money, you test the rule
on history — but a test will lie to
you if you let it.
Think of a dress rehearsal versus opening night; a
perfect rehearsal guarantees nothing.
On the chart, watch two curves. An overfit strategy
looks absolutely brilliant on the data it was tuned
on — that's in-sample — and then flattens or
falls apart on fresh data it never saw, walked
forward in time.
So, for example, you split your history into train,

validation, and test; you model every cost and
slippage;
and you never let the strategy peek at the
future.
In plain words, a good backtest attacks your idea
— it doesn't sell it to you. If it
only wins in one narrow setting, it's fragile.

The technical traps are overfitting, and
survivorship and look-ahead
bias.
Finally, going live — treat it like a pilot's
checklist before takeoff.

The most important code doesn't come after the
signal;
it sits right before the order.
Here it is, in order: the moment the rule
wants to trade, check that there's enough cash and
margin, that the order size is within limits, and
that you haven't blown your daily-loss cap — and
only then send the tagged order. If any check
fails, reject it and raise an alert.

For example, you paper-trade first to prove the
plumbing,
then go live with tiny size, watching for stale
feeds, rejected orders, and duplicates.

In plain words: size small, monitor everything, and
be
as ready to stop as you are to trade.

Technically, that's pre-trade risk management — and
very often,
the strongest line of code you write is the
one that prevents a trade.
So, the whole map.
A trading algorithm is a rule connected to data,
risk, routing, and monitoring.

The strategies differ — momentum, mean reversion,
breakout, execution
— but each can fail through costs, bad assumptions,
or a changing market.
India adds identity, rate limits, and audit trails.
Automation is not an edge.

Educational information from public sources, not
investment advice. Please
consult a S E B I-registered adviser.
Thanks for watching.
